summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application (sqli package): DAO layer, views/routes, auth utilities, middlewares, template rendering config, Jinja2 templates, service setup and config. The app is highly exploitable: an unauthenticated SQL injection exists in Student.create, output autoescaping is globally disabled yielding stored XSS, passwords are hashed with unsalted MD5, CSRF protection is defined but disabled, session cookies lack HttpOnly, and state-changing endpoints have no authorization. Coverage was the full Python source and templates; the vendored static JS/CSS and font assets were not audited.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: The query is built with Python %-formatting, splicing the raw student name directly into the SQL string instead of using a parameterized query. The value comes from request.post()['name'] in the students view (sqli/views.py:57), which handles POST /students/ with no authentication and no input validation. An unauthenticated attacker can inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. name=x'); DROP TABLE students;-- or a sub-select to exfiltrate the users table including pwd_hash) via the single-quoted interpolation.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  then cur.execute(q)  <- name is attacker-controlled data['name'] from POST /students/ (views.py:54-57). Contrast with the parameterized executes used elsewhere (e.g. course.py:47).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never build SQL with %/format/f-strings on user input.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescape
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so all template variables are rendered as raw HTML unless an explicit |e filter is applied. User-controlled, persisted values are rendered without escaping: review_text and course.title/course.description in course.jinja2 (lines 14-15, 22) and course.title/description in student.jinja2 (lines 19-20). Reviews can be created unauthenticated via POST /courses/{id}/review (views.py:129), so an attacker stores a <script> payload that executes in every visitor's browser (including admins), enabling session/account takeover.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  combined with course.jinja2:22 '{{ review.review_text }}' and course.jinja2:14-15 '{{ course.title }}' / '{{ course.description }}' rendered unescaped. review_text source: Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) from request.post().get('review_text') (views.py:121,129).
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (or autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','jinja2'])) in setup_jinja, and only use |safe for values known to be trusted HTML.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 in User.check_password
findings.description: User passwords are compared as unsalted MD5 hashes. MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: stored hashes (reachable via the SQL injection above) can be cracked with rainbow tables / GPU brute force almost instantly, and identical passwords yield identical hashes. This compromises all user accounts, including admins.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  — pwd_hash column stores a plain MD5 digest (no salt, no key stretching).
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash such as bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2 (e.g. passlib's argon2/bcrypt), and migrate stored hashes on next login.

findings.title: CSRF protection implemented but not enabled
findings.description: A working csrf_middleware is defined in sqli/middlewares.py (lines 25-38) and templates embed a _csrf_token, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no POST request's CSRF token is ever validated. All state-changing endpoints (login, create student, create course, create review, evaluate, logout) accept cross-site forged requests. Combined with cookie-based sessions this allows an attacker's page to perform actions as a logged-in victim.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware]  — csrf_middleware is commented out; csrf token validation in middlewares.py:26-37 is therefore never invoked.
findings.recommendation: Add csrf_middleware to the middlewares list so token validation runs on every POST (ensure the login form in index.jinja2 also carries _csrf_token).

findings.title: Session cookie set without HttpOnly flag
findings.description: RedisStorage is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored XSS above and the fact that the session identifies the authenticated user, an injected script can read document.cookie and exfiltrate the session, leading to full account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (the default is True) and also set secure=True and samesite='Lax'/'Strict' for the session cookie.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints
findings.description: The evaluate handler creates grade marks with no authentication or admin check, even though the UI only exposes the evaluate form to admins (course.jinja2:41 'if auth_user.is_admin'). The @authorize decorator exists (utils/auth.py) but is applied only to logout. The same missing-authorization pattern affects students (views.py:51-60, creates students), courses (views.py:83-93, creates courses) and review (views.py:111-131, creates reviews): any anonymous client can POST directly to these routes and mutate data. Representative instance is evaluate, which should be admin-only.
findings.evidence: @template('evaluate.jinja2')\nasync def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) — no get_auth_user/authorize guard; routes.py:21-23 registers POST .../evaluate/... with no auth. Same for students (routes.py:14), courses (routes.py:18), review (routes.py:28-30).
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize() / @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to the handlers that create or modify data (evaluate as admin-only), or enforce the checks inside each handler.

findings.title: Debug mode enabled on the aiohttp Application
findings.description: The Application is created with debug=True. In production this enables extra diagnostics (e.g. detailed warnings/tracebacks surfaced during request handling) and can leak internal details; it should not be hardcoded on. Low direct impact but it widens information disclosure.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False in production deployments.
